title: Starting strength training after breast surgery, and a back that hurts at night
objective: Start supervised, individualized progressive resistance training at least 1 month after breast cancer surgery, add aerobic exercise, and monitor tolerance at least weekly at first
secondaryObjectives: Treat new back pain in anyone with a cancer history as possible metastatic cord compression: back pain is the presenting symptom in 80 to 95%, often constant, worse at night and with coughing or sneezing
Escalate cord compression signs right away: bilateral leg symptoms, patchy weakness, multi-dermatome sensory loss, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence and gait change

sources.cite: NICE guideline NG234: Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression (2023), recommendations
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes. In people with past or current cancer, pain suggesting spinal metastases includes 'severe unremitting back pain', 'progressive back pain', 'back pain aggravated by straining (for example, coughing, sneezing or bowel movements)' and 'night-time back pain disturbing sleep'; symptoms suggesting cord compression include limb weakness, 'gait disturbance or difficulty walking', numbness or sensory loss, radicular pain and bladder or bowel dysfunction. With cord compression symptoms, 'Immediately contact the MSCC coordinator' and 'Treat this as an oncological emergency'; MRI 'as soon as possible (and always within 24 hours)'. A UK guideline; the case's clinic policy follows it.

brief.situation: 13:00 in an outpatient oncology rehabilitation clinic. You are the physical therapist. Mrs. Haddad, 58, had a left mastectomy with axillary node dissection 7 weeks ago for a recurrence of breast cancer first treated 6 years ago. Her surgeon cleared her for exercise. Today's plan: start her resistance and aerobic program.
handover: Shoulder range of motion is nearly full. No lymphedema at the last visit.
She mentioned 'a sore back from sleeping badly' to the front desk.
Clinic policy: suspected spinal cord compression in anyone with a cancer history goes to the emergency department now, with a call to her oncology team; tell her surgeon.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or test takes the time on its button. Decide what to check before loading, what it means and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The cord compression worsens slowly through the visit. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

parts.label: The program
parts.criteria: Resistance training after breast cancer surgery can start at least a month after surgery: supervised, individualized, progressive, with aerobic work and tolerance checked at least weekly at first; her arm is ready.
parts.modelAnswer: At seven weeks with no lymphedema she is ready for supervised, individualized progressive resistance training with aerobic work, checked at least weekly at first.

parts.label: Not today
parts.criteria: New constant mid-back pain for 2 weeks, worse at night and with coughing, in someone with a cancer history, now with heavy legs, falls, a sensory level and brisk reflexes: suspected metastatic cord compression, an oncological emergency; no loading; emergency department now and call oncology; tell the surgeon.
parts.modelAnswer: But not today. Constant mid-back pain for two weeks that wakes her and hurts with coughing, with heavy legs, two trips, a sensory level and brisk reflexes, in someone with a cancer history, is suspected metastatic spinal cord compression. No exercise; she goes to the emergency department now, lying flat, and I call her oncology team and tell her surgeon.

expertPath.text: Arm check: no lymphedema, shoulder ready. Ask about the back: constant, two weeks, worse at night and with coughing.
Ask about the legs: heavy, two trips, a numb band. Examine: weak hip flexors both sides, brisk reflexes, a sensory level.
No exercise. Emergency department now, lying flat; call her oncology team. Write the plan for later: supervised progressive resistance with weekly checks once cleared. Tell her surgeon.

collapse.headline: Her legs gave way
collapse.body: New back pain in anyone with a cancer history is cord compression until shown otherwise. Ask about the legs and examine before loading.

delayed.headline: Sent home with cord compression
delayed.body: Leg weakness, a sensory level and gait change with that back pain are an oncological emergency: now, not next week.

sentNow.headline: Sent now
sentNow.body: You knew she was ready for supervised resistance training, screened before loading, recognized suspected cord compression and sent her the same hour. That is the expert path.

sentGaps.headline: Sent, with gaps
sentGaps.body: Check whether the leg questions came before any loading and how long the decision took.

time_up.headline: Still in the clinic
time_up.body: The exercise plan can wait; the spine cannot.

scoring.modelReasoning: Seven weeks after breast cancer surgery with no lymphedema, she is ready for supervised, individualized progressive resistance training with aerobic work, checked at least weekly at first. But new constant mid-back pain for two weeks that is worse at night and with coughing, in someone with a cancer history, suggests spinal metastases, and heavy legs, falls, a sensory level and brisk reflexes suggest cord compression: an oncological emergency with MRI within 24 hours. No loading today; emergency department now with a call to her oncology team, and tell her surgeon. The program starts once her spine is cleared.

choices.label: Constant or progressive pain, worse at night or with coughing or straining
Stiffness that eases within minutes of getting up

backQ.explain: Night pain, pain with straining and progressive or unremitting pain suggest spinal metastases in people with cancer.
